content: 1. Staff costs are determined by measuring the time staff spend on specific tasks using timesheets, direct observation, or interviews. The cost is calculated based on their salaries or wages. 2. Supplies are quantified by assessing the amount of consumables used, and their cost is derived from annual expenditure or the price of the consumables. 3. Drug costs are calculated by identifying the number and type of drugs or regimens used, with the price based on the current cost of the medications. 4. Diagnostic test costs are determined by counting the number and type of diagnostic tests or supplies used, with the price based on the current cost of these tests or supplies. 5. Additional costs may include calibration of instruments, chemicals, reagents, cash transfer administration, and quality assurance activities. 6. Data collection for tuberculosis (TB) interventions should be designed to capture both capital and recurrent inputs, such as community outreach, household visits, or school-based activities. 7. Mapping interventions involves defining and classifying interventions according to standardized definitions, then mapping the available interventions and technologies at each facility level to identify where costs will be captured. 8. A blank Data Collection Tool should be used for each facility to record descriptions of the health facility, service utilization, and overhead items. This tool includes default lists of staff types, equipment, consumables, chemicals, reagents, and drugs used in TB interventions. 9. Inputs for unit cost calculations are categorized into capital (e.g., building space, vehicles, equipment, training) and recurrent inputs (e.g., staff costs, supplies). Diagnostic testing and medication costs are added later due to their variability. 10. Costing approaches include bottom-up and top-down methods. Bottom-up costing involves detailed measurement of all resources used in providing a specific health service, while top-down costing allocates facility expenditures to specific cost centers. 11. Bottom-up costing uses methods such as interviews, time-motion studies, observation, or work sampling to estimate resource use. This approach captures inefficiencies in the production process. 12. Top-down costing allocates shared resources based on explicit criteria, such as usage of inputs, and considers inefficiencies in capacity. It is often used for complex organizations or aggregated costs. 13. Staff time is measured by multiplying the cost of staff time per minute (derived from employment costs and annual working minutes) by the time spent on TB services, collected through observation or interviews. 14. Resource valuation involves quantifying and valuing all identified resources for each facility. This includes current prices for consumables, medical equipment, furniture, and other inputs. 15. Total costs are estimated by multiplying unit costs by total utilization over a specific period. For example, the cost of TB hospitalization can be calculated using national averages or facility expenditure accounts. 16. The Value TB Costing Tool Suite, developed in Microsoft Excel, provides a standardized framework for costing TB interventions. It includes tools for data collection, data entry, and unit cost generation, along with draft informed consent forms. 17. The Data Collection Tool records quantity and price data for TB interventions at a facility, capturing both bottom-up and top-down inputs such as staff time, training, building space, equipment, drugs, and supplies. 18. The Data Entry Tool is used by analysts to clean data from the Data Collection Tool and generate unit costs for delivering TB services using both bottom-up and top-down methodologies. 19. Bottom-up unit costs are calculated by combining prices and quantities for all inputs, while top-down unit costs are derived using step-down accounting and allocation based on space or service statistics. 20. The Value TB Costing Tool Suite is adaptable to any TB service costing exercise and simplifies data collection and analysis for researchers.
